_comment: Declared, reasoned differences between packages/zip and Python's zipfile. Every entry must say WHY. Two things are never declarable: sourcesAgree:false (the package contradicting itself), and a crash.
_format: Keys are 'policy:stricter-than-python' (a blanket policy, see below), 'policy:version-needed-is-advisory' and 'policy:refuses-unsafe-names' (blanket policies), 'lenient:<basename>' (we accepted an archive Python refused -- the dangerous direction, declarable only per archive), or 'name:<ours>:<theirs>' (a name decoded differently).
policy:stricter-than-python: We refuse archives that Python's zipfile recovers from. Measured on the corpus, this covers three damage classes: an end-of-central-directory record whose declared comment length does not land at end of file; a central-directory offset pointing past the end; and an entry count larger than the directory actually holds. In each case the archive contradicts itself, and APPNOTE.TXT 6.3.10 specifies only how a WELL-FORMED archive is laid out -- it does not require a reader to reconstruct a broken one, so both readings are permitted and this is a policy choice rather than a defect. The choice is to refuse, for two reasons. First, this package is built to be pointed at untrusted input, and a reader that guesses what a self-inconsistent archive 'meant' is exactly how two readers end up disagreeing about what an archive contains -- the confusion that makes a scanner and an extractor see different files. Second, the strictness is only ever in the safe direction: the opposite case, where we accept something Python refuses, is NOT covered by this policy and fails the diff per archive, because that is the direction in which we might be the ones getting it wrong. Per entry, the same policy also covers four refusals that Python does not make, which the package makes for the reasons its own source gives. (1) A local header's copies of the name, the method and the sizes must agree with the central directory's. The sizes are compared only when general-purpose flag bit 3 is clear, since a data descriptor then carries the real sizes, and not where a ZIP64 sentinel defers the value. The reason, in entry.mfb: two copies that say different things are ambiguous, and an ambiguous archive is refused rather than resolved in one reader's favour. (2) A directory entry's local header is held to the same rule as a file's, for the same reason: it is another copy of the same record. (3) An entry's footprint, which overlap detection uses, runs from its local header through its name, extra field and data, so the footprints are checked from the central directory alone; in central.mfb, two entries sharing bytes is the shape of a zip bomb and a confusion vector. (4) General-purpose flag bits 0 (encrypted), 5 (patched data), 6 (strong encryption) and 13 (masked local header) are refused in either copy of the flags, because inflating such data anyway would return something that is not the entry's contents (entry.mfb, requireSupportedFlags).
policy:version-needed-is-advisory: Python's zipfile refuses any archive whose central-directory 'version needed to extract' field exceeds 6.3 (NotImplementedError: 'zip file version N'). We ignore that field and validate the features the archive actually uses instead -- the compression method, the encryption flag, and whether ZIP64 records are present and well-formed -- refusing on those concretely. APPNOTE.TXT 6.3.10 §4.4.3 defines the field as the minimum version needed to extract, and it is advisory: it is set by the writer, is frequently wrong in archives found in the wild, and says nothing a reader cannot determine for itself by looking. Refusing on a claim rather than on a capability would reject archives this package can read perfectly well, while catching nothing it could not already catch. This exception is keyed on Python's exact message so it cannot quietly cover any other refusal; every other 'we accepted, Python refused' case still fails the diff.
policy:refuses-unsafe-names: Extraction refuses an archive that contains a name an independent extractor would sanitise, overwrite or fail on, instead of resolving it. The classes are: an absolute path (a leading '/'); a '..' component; a backslash; a Windows drive prefix ('C:'); two entries that extract to one path; and a file where another entry needs a directory. Python's zipfile.extractall does not refuse any of these: it strips a leading '/' and drops '..' and '.' components, so the file lands at a path the archive did not name; it overwrites on a duplicate, so the last entry wins; and it fails partway through on a file-versus-directory collision. A backslash and a drive prefix are kept literally on POSIX but are separators and drive-relative paths on Windows, so the same archive lands in different places on different hosts. Refusing before the first byte is written is the one answer that gives the same result everywhere and leaves the directory as it was. This policy covers ONLY a refusal with errorCode::ErrInvalidPath or errorCode::ErrInvalidFormat on an archive that contains one of these names. A refusal for any other reason, and an archive with none of them, is not covered and fails the extract gate.
